sources.title: CommScope Category 6A Cables
sources.scope: Read the manufacturer explanation that Cat 6A structured cabling supports 10 Gigabit Ethernet channels up to 100 m. This is conditional channel capability, not a guarantee for every device, optic, or installation.

sources.title: IANA Service Name and Port Number Registry

Registry reservations do not imply every service uses all registered transports or that a port guarantees security.

pages.title: Risk and Security Goals
notes: Asset value and exposure shape security risk.
Threat is a possible harmful actor or event.
Vulnerability is a weakness that can be exploited.
Exploit is a method or code using that weakness.
Risk combines likelihood and impact in context.
Unpatched public software raises exposure, not certainty.
Insiders, mistakes, suppliers, and outsiders create risk.
Zero-day is unknown to responsible defenders or vendors.
Confidentiality limits disclosure to authorized parties.

pages.title: Controls and Malware Defense
notes: Integrity means preserving data accuracy and completeness.
Availability means timely access to authorized users.
Account lifecycle removes stale users and excess access.
Authentication verifies a claimed identity or authenticator.
Authorization decides allowed actions; permissions enforce it.
Encryption obscures content without the required key.
Antivirus detects known or suspicious patterns; misses occur.
Mail and web filters reduce risky links and attachments.
Patching removes known flaws after suitable testing.
Disable unused services; verify needed network flows first.

pages.title: Availability and Attack Paths
notes: DoS denies service by exhausting a constrained resource.
Floods may saturate links or consume server request capacity.
Protocol attacks can exhaust connection or state tables.
Application floods consume workers, memory, or CPU.
DDoS distributes traffic across many compromised devices.
Botnets coordinate infected devices for distributed attacks.
Distributed sources complicate filtering and attribution.
Phishing impersonates trusted senders to prompt unsafe action.
Spoofing forges apparent sender, address, or device identity.

pages.title: Integrity, Identity, and Recovery
notes: Poisoning corrupts trusted lookup data, such as DNS cache.
Hash maps data to a fixed-size digest; it is not encryption.
A trusted digest comparison can reveal changed file contents.
An unauthenticated hash does not prove who supplied the file.
Digital signature uses private key; public key verifies it.
Signatures prove integrity/key origin, not secrecy.
Certificate binds identity and public key under issuer policy.
Validate certificate chain, name, validity, and trust.
MFA uses distinct factors; RADIUS supports remote access.
SSO reuses login; TACACS+ separates device AAA functions.

practice.prompt: Explain the four terms in a risk example involving an unpatched server.
practice.answer: The threat is a possible attacker/event, the flaw is the vulnerability, exploit is the method used, and risk reflects likelihood and impact for that exposed asset.

practice.prompt: Why is a hash neither encryption nor proof of author?
practice.answer: It produces a digest for change detection, not reversible secrecy; absent a trusted signature or channel an attacker can replace both content and digest.

pages.title: Malware and Social Engineering
notes: Virus attaches to host content and runs when executed.
Worm self-propagates; it need not attach to a host file.
Trojan disguises harmful code as useful software.
Logic bomb triggers when a time or condition is met.
Ransomware blocks or encrypts data for extortion.
Phishing arrives through email, text, call, or fake site.
Urgency and unexpected credential requests are warning signs.
Spoofing falsifies identity; verify sender independently.
Poisoning alters trusted data so later lookups mislead users.

pages.title: Resilient Defensive Layers
notes: Filter risky links/files; scanners cannot catch every sample.
Verify payment or password requests through known channels.
Patch exposed systems and retire unsupported software.
Least privilege limits damage from stolen accounts or malware.
Segmentation restricts paths to critical systems.
Backups aid recovery; isolate copies from normal admin access.
Test restores because untested copies may be incomplete.
Close unused ports only after checking service dependencies.
Firewall rules filter traffic; they cannot stop all attacks.
Monitor logs and alerts; sensors require review and response.

pages.title: DoS Mechanics
notes: A volumetric flood consumes available link bandwidth.
A protocol flood consumes connection or device state.
An application flood forces costly valid-looking work.
Reflection sends third-party replies to a victim.
Amplification makes replies larger than triggering requests.
Forged source addresses can obscure origins in some floods.
Botnet DDoS adds traffic from many compromised endpoints.
A firewall cannot restore a saturated upstream link.
Outages deny service to legitimate users.

pages.title: Mitigation and Residual Risk
notes: Upstream filtering or scrubbing can remove attack traffic.
Rate limits reduce abusive request rates but need tuning.
Redundancy and capacity help only within design limits.
Broad filters may block legitimate clients too.
Coordinate with providers when circuit capacity is exceeded.
Report phishing; do not click, reply, or share approval codes.
Antivirus and filters complement user verification.
Preserve logs and follow incident response procedures.
No single control guarantees service or prevents compromise.
Review residual risk as systems and attacker methods change.

practice.prompt: A service loses access during a large distributed flood. What is the mechanism and a likely response?
practice.answer: DDoS sends traffic from many compromised systems, possibly exhausting link, state, or app capacity. Upstream scrubbing may be needed if the circuit is saturated; rate limits help only for suitable traffic.

practice.prompt: A caller urgently requests an MFA code to prevent account closure. How should staff respond?
practice.answer: Treat as possible phishing/impersonation, never disclose the code, verify using a known contact route, and report it. Encryption does not stop a user giving a secret to an impostor.

pages.title: File and Mail Protocols
notes: FTP transfers files through control and data connections.
FTP control commonly listens on TCP port 21 by default.
FTP active/passive modes change data connection ports.
Plain FTP does not protect credentials or contents in transit.
FTPS adds TLS to FTP; SFTP is file transfer over SSH.
SFTP commonly uses TCP port 22, the SSH default.
SMTP transfers mail between systems and supports submission.
SMTP relay commonly uses TCP 25; submission often uses 587.
TCP 465 often means implicit-TLS submission; configs vary.

pages.title: DNS, DHCP, and IP
notes: DNS answers name queries with records such as IP addresses.
DNS commonly uses UDP 53; TCP 53 is also required.
DHCP supplies leases and network settings to hosts.
DHCPv4 commonly uses UDP 67 server and 68 client.
A lease may include address, mask, router, and DNS server.
DHCP relay can carry client requests across routed subnets.
DHCP address is host configuration, not permanent identity.
DNS name resolution does not itself route packets to a host.
Gateway forwards traffic beyond the local IP subnet.
Stale or poisoned DNS data can direct clients incorrectly.

pages.title: Transport and Port Defaults
notes: TCP provides an ordered byte stream with retransmission.
TCP setup and recovery add overhead; delivery is not instant.
UDP sends datagrams without TCP delivery/order guarantees.
Applications may add reliability above UDP when needed.
IP carries packets; TCP/UDP ports identify endpoints.
HTTP commonly uses TCP 80; HTTPS commonly TCP 443.
SSH commonly uses TCP 22; service ports can be changed.
DNS uses UDP or TCP 53; blocking TCP can break functions.
NTP commonly uses UDP 123; defaults are not exclusive rules.

pages.title: NAT and Secure Service Use
notes: NAT maps IP addresses between address realms.
NAPT also maps transport ports for multiple inside hosts.
Home gateways commonly share one public IPv4 address.
Translation conserves addresses; it does not encrypt packets.
NAT is not a firewall policy or authentication mechanism.
A stateful firewall separately permits or denies flows.
Inbound reachability may need mapping and explicit policy.
TLS aims to protect channels from eavesdropping and tampering.
Use secure transfer; configure TLS and verify peer identity.
Service configuration, not port number, determines exposure.

practice.prompt: A workstation has no address and cannot look up a server name. Which roles should be checked?
practice.answer: Check DHCP lease and options for IP, gateway, and DNS server; DNS resolves the name, then IP routing and gateway carry traffic to the destination.

practice.prompt: Does a gateway using NAT automatically make an exposed service safe?
practice.answer: No. NAT rewrites addresses/ports and may limit unsolicited inbound mapping, but it is not encryption or access policy; a firewall, authentication, patching, and service configuration remain necessary.

pages.title: Wireless Generations and Bands
notes: 802.11b uses 2.4 GHz DSSS; max PHY rate is 11 Mb/s.
802.11a uses 5 GHz OFDM; max PHY rate is 54 Mb/s.
802.11g uses 2.4 GHz OFDM; max PHY rate is 54 Mb/s.
802.11n (Wi-Fi 4) supports 2.4/5 GHz and MIMO.
802.11ac (Wi-Fi 5) operates in 5 GHz bands.
802.11ax (Wi-Fi 6) supports 2.4 and 5 GHz operation.
Wi-Fi 6E adds 6 GHz where permitted and supported.
802.11be (Wi-Fi 7) adds multi-link in capable devices.
Max PHY rates require matching channel and radio capability.

pages.title: Wireless Range and Throughput
notes: There is no single universal indoor Wi-Fi range figure.
Band, walls, antennas, power, and receivers affect reach.
2.4 GHz often travels farther through walls than 5/6 GHz.
2.4 GHz is often more congested; local spectrum matters.
Channel width, streams, and interference affect PHY rate.
App throughput is below PHY rate due to overhead/contention.
Clients share airtime; slow stations reduce capacity.
Regulatory domain limits channels and transmit power.
Survey user locations and load before estimating coverage.
A repeater can extend reach but consumes airtime or adds hops.

pages.title: Ethernet PHY and Medium
notes: 10BASE-T is 10 Mb/s over twisted-pair copper, up to 100 m.
100BASE-TX is 100 Mb/s copper, up to 100 m channel.
1000BASE-T carries 1 Gb/s over four pairs, up to 100 m.
10GBASE-T can reach 100 m on Cat 6A compliant channel.
Cat 6 10GBASE-T reach depends on channel and alien crosstalk.
1000BASE-SX uses multimode fiber; reach varies by grade.
1000BASE-LX reach depends on optics and fiber type.
10GBASE-SR uses multimode fiber; distance depends on fiber.
IEEE PHY, optics, connectors, and loss set fiber reach.

pages.title: Routing and Wireless Protection
notes: OSPF is link-state routing within an autonomous system.
OSPF routers build topology databases and calculate paths.
BGP exchanges inter-AS prefixes and paths for policy.
BGP is an IETF Standards Track protocol.
EIGRP uses DUAL, a distance-vector-based routing algorithm.
RFC 7868 is Informational, not an IETF Standards Track spec.
WPA2 deployments can use AES-CCMP; avoid legacy TKIP.
WPA3-Personal SAE strengthens resistance to offline guessing.
WPA3 connections require Protected Management Frames.
Negotiated security depends on AP/client configuration.

practice.prompt: Why can Wi-Fi 6E not guarantee better speed or a fixed larger range?
practice.answer: 6 GHz support and PHY maxima depend on client/AP capability, permitted channels, interference, channel width, walls, power and shared airtime. Actual coverage and throughput require local measurement.

practice.prompt: Which protocol suits internal topology routing versus inter-provider reachability, and what is EIGRP's RFC status?
practice.answer: OSPF is an intra-AS link-state protocol; BGP exchanges inter-AS reachability under policy. EIGRP uses DUAL, and RFC 7868 is Informational rather than Standards Track.

lab.title: Paper network protocol trace
steps: Diagram a client obtaining DHCP settings and resolving a DNS name.
Trace a TCP or UDP service to a gateway and describe NAT separately from firewall policy.
Compare OSPF internal routes with BGP inter-AS advertisements and EIGRP RFC status.
Estimate wireless deployment only after recording band, obstacles, client capabilities, and load.
Select a named Ethernet PHY and check its copper or fiber medium assumptions.
Compare WPA2/WPA3 configuration and note device compatibility; use no live attack traffic.
expected: DHCP, DNS, IP, and gateway roles are distinguished.
Port defaults are not treated as exclusive or protective.
Routing protocol scope and standards status are correct.
RF range and throughput are expressed conditionally.
Ethernet reach is tied to PHY and medium.

limitations: Cisco RF guide (2024) includes generation/link-rate table, but table cites secondary material and its maxima are not guarantees. Cisco Ethernet cable guide is older and supports only listed PHY/cable cases; validate other media/reaches against exact transceiver datasheets. WPA3 notes use Cisco 17.15 configuration guide and apply only to supported combinations.
